items.prose: A lab tests 60 genes for a link with a disease, one test per gene. Treat the 60 tests as independent. The eight smallest p-values, sorted, are 0.0004, 0.0021, 0.0055, 0.0058, 0.0090, 0.0096, 0.0190 and 0.034. The other 52 are all above 0.2.

parts.question: The lab wants at most a 10% chance of any false link across its 60 tests. What bar does Bonferroni give each gene? Give 6 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Bonferroni divides the family's target by the number of tests.

byKey.unadjusted: That is the family's target itself. Each of the 60 tests gets a share of it: $\tfrac{0.10}{60}$.
byKey.times-m: You multiplied by 60. Bonferroni divides, so that the 60 bars together add to at most 0.10.
byKey.five-percent: You used 5%. This lab's target is 10%, so the bar is $\tfrac{0.10}{60}$.

explain.text: Each of the 60 tests gets one sixtieth of the 10% budget, 0.001667. By the union bound, the 60 bars add to 0.10. So the chance of any false link is at most 10%.

parts.question: Using the bar 0.001667 from part 1, how many genes does Bonferroni reject? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Only 0.0004 is at most 0.001667. The next, 0.0021, is above it.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each p-value with 0.001667.

byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value under 0.10. Bonferroni compares each with 0.001667.
byKey.bh: That is BH's count, with a rising bar. Bonferroni holds every gene to the single bar 0.001667.

explain.text: Bonferroni uses one bar for all 60 genes. Only the smallest p-value, 0.0004, falls under it, so it rejects 1.

parts.question: BH at $q = 0.10$ gives rank $k$ the bar $k \times 0.001667$, $k$ times the bar from part 1. It rejects every rank up to the largest one under its bar. How many genes does BH reject? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: Ranks 1 and 2 pass. Rank 3 fails (0.0055 against 0.005) and rank 4 passes (0.0058 against 0.00667). Rank 5 fails (0.0090 against 0.00833) and rank 6 passes (0.0096 against 0.01). Ranks 7 and 8 fail, so BH rejects 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the largest rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le k \times 0.001667$, then reject ranks 1 to $k$.

byKey.first-fail: You stopped at rank 3, where 0.0055 is above 0.005. BH keeps going: rank 6, 0.0096, is under 0.01.
byKey.bonferroni: That is Bonferroni's count. BH's bar rises with the rank: 0.001667, 0.003333, 0.005 and so on.
byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value under 0.10. BH's bars for ranks 1 to 8 run from 0.001667 to 0.01333.
byKey.count-passes: You counted the ranks that pass their own bars. BH rejects every rank up to the largest one that passes, so ranks 3 and 5 come in too.

explain.text: The bars for ranks 1 to 8 rise in steps of 0.001667, to 0.01333. The largest rank under its bar is 6, so BH rejects the six smallest, ranks 3 and 5 included.

parts.question: BH kept 6 genes at $q = 0.10$. Rank 6 stays in when $p_{(6)} \le \tfrac{6q}{60}$. Using $p_{(6)} = 0.0096$, what is the smallest $q$ that keeps it? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.no-divide: You multiplied 0.0096 by 60 and left out the division by 6. Rank 6's bar is $\tfrac{6q}{60}$, so $q = \tfrac{60 \times 0.0096}{6}$.
byKey.rank-five: That is the $q$ that rank 5 needs, $\tfrac{60 \times 0.0090}{5}$. Rank 6 is the one asked about, and it needs less.
byKey.bar: That is rank 6's bar at $q = 0.10$. The question asks for $q$, so solve $0.0096 = \tfrac{6q}{60}$.

explain.text: Rank 6 stays in once $q \ge \tfrac{60 \times 0.0096}{6} = 0.096$. That is just under 0.10, so BH at 10% keeps it. Ranks 3 and 5, which alone would need $q = 0.11$ and $q = 0.108$, come in with it.

parts.question: Using parts 2 to 4, which statement about the two lists is right?

options.text: Bonferroni keeps the chance of any false link at most 10%; BH keeps the average share of false links at most 10%
Both lists keep the chance of any false link at 10%, so the longer list is better
options.why: BH controls the false discovery rate, an average share. The chance of at least one false link among BH's 6 can be higher than 10%.

options.text: BH's list leaves out rank 3, since 0.0055 fails its bar
options.why: BH rejects every rank up to the largest one that passes. Rank 6 passes, so ranks 1 to 6 are all in, rank 3 included.

options.text: Raising $q$ to 0.20 would leave BH's list unchanged
options.why: At $q = 0.20$ the bar for rank 7 is 0.02333, and 0.0190 is under it, so the list grows.

feedback.correct: Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate at 10%. BH controls the false discovery rate at 10% for independent tests, so it can afford a longer list: 6 genes against 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what each method promises: a chance of any false link, or an average share.

byKey.same: BH controls the false discovery rate, an average share. The chance of at least one false link among BH's 6 can be higher than 10%.
byKey.rank-three: BH rejects every rank up to the largest one that passes. Rank 6 passes, so ranks 1 to 6 are all in, rank 3 included.
byKey.q-same: At $q = 0.20$ the bar for rank 7 is 0.02333, and 0.0190 is under it, so the list grows.

explain.text: Bonferroni holds the chance of even one false link to at most 10%, which costs power. BH lets a few false links in, on average at most 10% of its list, and finds more.

items.prose: A pension consultant screens 8 fund managers with independent track records. She tests each annualised Sharpe ratio against 0, one-sided, and uses BH to hold the false discovery rate at 10%. Manager H has a Sharpe ratio of 0.9 over 9 years.

parts.question: What is manager H's $t$ statistic? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the Sharpe ratio by the square root of the years.

byKey.over-root: You divided by $\sqrt 9$. The standard error of a Sharpe ratio is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt T}$, so $t$ multiplies by $\sqrt T$.
byKey.times-t: You multiplied by 9 years. The $t$ statistic grows with $\sqrt T = 3$.

explain.text: Over 9 years the Sharpe ratio has standard error $\tfrac{1}{3}$. So 0.9 sits $0.9 \times 3 = 2.7$ standard errors above 0.

parts.question: Using $t = 2.7$ from part 1 and $\Phi(2.7) = 0.9965$, what is H's one-sided p-value? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the upper tail beyond $t = 2.7$.

byKey.two-sided: You doubled the tail. Her test asks only whether the Sharpe ratio is above 0.
byKey.lower: That is the area below 2.7. The one-sided p-value is the area above it.

explain.text: The upper tail beyond 2.7 holds 0.0035. A manager with no skill would show a record this good fewer than 4 times in 1,000.

parts.question: The other seven p-values are 0.0006, 0.014, 0.052, 0.058, 0.09, 0.31 and 0.62. With H's p-value, 0.0035 from part 2, BH at $q = 0.10$ compares the $k$-th smallest with $\tfrac{0.10k}{8} = 0.0125k$. How many managers does it reject?

feedback.correct: Sorted: 0.0006, 0.0035, 0.014, 0.052, 0.058. Ranks 1 to 3 pass, and rank 4 fails (0.052 against 0.05). Rank 5 passes (0.058 against 0.0625), and no later rank does, so BH rejects 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sort the eight p-values, then find the largest rank $k$ with $p_{(k)} \le 0.0125k$.

byKey.first-fail: You stopped at rank 4, where 0.052 is above 0.05. BH keeps going: rank 5, 0.058, is under 0.0625.
byKey.bonferroni: Two is what Bonferroni at 0.0125 keeps, and what BH gives if H's p is taken as 0.9965. With p = 0.0035, the largest rank under its bar is 5.
byKey.unadjusted: That counts every p-value up to 0.10. BH's bar for rank $k$ is only $0.0125k$.

explain.text: H's 0.0035 sorts second. The largest rank under its bar is 5, so BH backs five managers, the one at rank 4 included.

items.prose: An online shop tests 18 new checkout pages against its current page, each with a two-sided test at 5% on the same month of traffic. Treat the 18 tests as independent, and suppose no page truly differs. The shop launches every page that passes, and each launch costs £4,000 in engineering time.

parts.question: How many launches does the shop expect from the 18 pages? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Each page passes with chance 0.05, and expectations add: $18 \times 0.05 = 0.9$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the number of pages by the chance that one passes.

byKey.one-sided: You used one tail, 0.025. A two-sided test passes a null page with chance 0.05.
byKey.all-pages: That is the number of pages. Each launches only if it passes, which is 5% of the time.
byKey.complement: That is how many pages fail, $18 \times 0.95$. The shop launches the ones that pass, at 5%.

explain.text: Each of the 18 null pages passes with chance 0.05. So the shop expects $18 \times 0.05 = 0.9$ launches, nearly one useless page a month.

parts.question: Using 0.9 launches from part 1, what do the useless launches cost the shop on average? Give pounds, as a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the expected launches by the cost of one.

byKey.all-pages: That launches all 18 pages. The shop launches only the ones that pass, 0.9 on average.
byKey.one-launch: That is one launch. The shop expects 0.9 of them, not 1.
byKey.thousands: You left out the thousand. One launch costs £4,000.

explain.text: Expected cost is the expected number of launches times the cost of one: 0.9 times £4,000 is £3,600. Every one of those launches is a page that does nothing.

parts.question: The shop now uses the Bonferroni bar, for a 5% chance of any false launch across the 18 pages. What bar does each test use? Give 6 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Bonferroni divides the family's target by the number of tests.

byKey.unadjusted: That is the family's target itself. Each of the 18 tests gets a share of it: $\tfrac{0.05}{18}$.
byKey.times-n: You multiplied by 18. Bonferroni divides, so that the 18 bars together add to at most 0.05.
byKey.sidak: That is the Šidák bar, $1 - 0.95^{1/18}$, a little larger. The question asks for Bonferroni: $\tfrac{0.05}{18}$.

explain.text: Bonferroni gives each of the 18 tests one eighteenth of the 5% budget, 0.002778. That bar is stricter than 0.05 for every page.

parts.question: Using the bar 0.002778 from part 3, what is the chance of at least one useless launch? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: All 18 stay quiet with chance $(1 - 0.002778)^{18} = 0.9512$, so at least one launch has chance $1 - 0.9512 = 0.0488$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the chance that every page stays quiet at the new bar, then take the complement.

byKey.bound: 0.05 is the union bound, which Bonferroni guarantees, and what the Šidák bar gives. With the bar 0.002778 the exact chance is a little lower.
byKey.no-complement: That is $0.997222^{18}$, the chance that all 18 stay quiet. Take its complement.
byKey.carried: That is the chance at 5% per page, $1 - 0.95^{18}$. At 0.002778 per page the 18 quiet chances are each 0.997222.

explain.text: Each useless page now launches with chance 0.002778. The chance that none does is 0.9512. So the chance of at least one is 0.0488, just under the 0.05 budget.

parts.question: Under the bar from part 3, the expected waste is $18 \times 0.002778 \times$ £4,000 = £200. Now suppose a few pages really are better. Using parts 2 to 4, what does the stricter bar cost the shop?

options.text: Pages that do improve checkout must also clear the stricter bar, so fewer of them are found
Nothing: a stricter bar only removes useless launches
options.why: A page that truly helps must pass the same stricter test. It is more likely to be missed.

options.text: The shop can never launch a page again
options.why: A page with a p-value under 0.002778 still passes. The bar is strict, not closed.

options.text: Nothing, because the expected waste is now £0, so anything that passes is safe to launch
options.why: Expected waste is £200, not £0, and the chance of at least one useless launch is still 0.0488.

feedback.correct: Expected waste falls from £3,600 to £200, and the chance of any useless launch from 0.6028 to 0.0488. The price is power: a better page must now clear 0.002778.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the same stricter bar does to a page that really is better.

byKey.free: A page that truly helps must pass the same stricter test. It is more likely to be missed.
byKey.never: A page with a p-value under 0.002778 still passes. The bar is strict, not closed.
byKey.safe: Expected waste is £200, not £0, and the chance of at least one useless launch is still 0.0488.

explain.text: A stricter bar removes most useless launches, but it applies to good pages too. A page with a real gain is found less often, so the shop trades power for a cleaner list.

items.prose: A medical field has tested 400 candidate biomarkers, each with a two-sided $z$ test. Suppose 380 have no effect and 20 have a real one, and treat the 400 tests as independent. The field is choosing a bar $|z| > c$. For each bar the table gives the chance that a null passes and the chance that a real biomarker passes. At $c = 2.5$ they are 0.0124 and 0.90. At 2.8 they are 0.0051 and 0.84. At 3.1 they are 0.0019 and 0.75. At 3.5 they are 0.00047 and 0.61.

parts.question: The field wants to expect at most 1 false find from its 380 nulls. How large can a null's pass chance be? Give 6 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Expected false finds are $380 \times$ the pass chance. Setting that to 1 gives $\tfrac{1}{380} = 0.002632$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Expected false finds are the number of nulls times the pass chance of one null.

byKey.over-400: You divided by all 400. Only the 380 nulls can give a false find, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{380}$.
byKey.times: You multiplied 1 by 380. Expected false finds are 380 times a null's pass chance, so that chance is $\tfrac{1}{380}$.
byKey.five-percent: You divided 0.05 by 380, the Bonferroni bar for a 5% chance of any false find. The target here is one expected false find: $\tfrac{1}{380}$.

explain.text: Each of the 380 nulls passes with the same chance, and expectations add. So $380 \times \text{chance} \le 1$ needs a chance of at most $\tfrac{1}{380} = 0.002632$.

parts.question: Using 0.002632 from part 1, which is the lowest bar with a null pass chance at most that?

options.why: At 2.5 a null passes with chance 0.0124, so 380 nulls give $380 \times 0.0124 = 4.712$ false finds, over 1.
At 2.8 a null passes with chance 0.0051, so 380 nulls give $380 \times 0.0051 = 1.938$ false finds, over 1.
3.5 keeps a null at 0.00047, under 0.002632, but it is not the lowest bar that does. A bar higher than needed costs power: 0.61 against 0.75.

feedback.correct: At 3.1 a null passes with chance 0.0019, under 0.002632. At 2.8 it is 0.0051, which is over.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first bar in the table, from the lowest, whose null pass chance is at most 0.002632.

byKey.c25: At 2.5 a null passes with chance 0.0124, so 380 nulls give $380 \times 0.0124 = 4.712$ false finds, over 1.
byKey.c28: At 2.8 a null passes with chance 0.0051, so 380 nulls give $380 \times 0.0051 = 1.938$ false finds, over 1.
byKey.c35: 3.5 keeps a null at 0.00047, under 0.002632, but it is not the lowest bar that does. A bar higher than needed costs power: 0.61 against 0.75.

explain.text: Of the table's bars, 3.1 is the lowest that meets it, with 0.0019. A higher bar only costs power.

parts.question: At the bar 3.1, how many of the 20 real biomarkers does the field expect to find? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: A real biomarker passes the bar 3.1 with chance 0.75, so $20 \times 0.75 = 15$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the 20 real biomarkers by the chance that a real one passes at 3.1.

byKey.old-bar: That uses 0.90, the pass chance at 2.5. At 3.1 a real biomarker passes with chance 0.75.
byKey.all-real: That counts all 20. A real biomarker passes only 75% of the time at this bar.
byKey.next-bar: That uses 0.61, the pass chance at 3.5. The bar chosen in part 2 is 3.1, with chance 0.75.
byKey.lower-bar: That uses 0.84, the pass chance at 2.8. The bar chosen in part 2 is 3.1, with chance 0.75.

explain.text: Real effects are found with chance 0.75 at this bar. So the field expects $20 \times 0.75 = 15$ real finds, and misses 5.

parts.question: Using 15 real finds from part 3, what share of all finds at 3.1 are false? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the false finds from the 380 nulls, then divide by all the finds, false and real.

byKey.true-share: That is the share of finds that are real. The question asks for the false share, $\tfrac{0.722}{15.722}$.
byKey.over-400: You divided the false finds by all 400 biomarkers. The share is out of the finds, $0.722 + 15$.
byKey.no-power: You counted all 20 real biomarkers as finds. At this bar only 15 of them pass.

explain.text: At the bar 3.1 the field expects 15.722 finds, of which 0.722 are false. So about 4.6% of its finds are false.

parts.question: Using part 4, what does the false share 0.0459 tell the field?

options.text: About 1 in 22 finds is expected to be false, yet at least one false find is about as likely as not
The chance of at least one false find across the field is 0.0459
options.why: That is the share of finds that are false. With 380 independent nulls at 0.0019 each, the chance of at least one false find is $1 - 0.9981^{380} \approx 0.51$.

options.text: Each find is false with chance 0.0019, the null pass chance at this bar
options.why: 0.0019 is the chance that a null passes, not the share of finds that are false.

options.text: The bar has removed every false find, so none is expected any more
options.why: 0.722 false finds are still expected, and one or more happens in about half of all fields.

feedback.correct: False finds are about 4.6% of the finds. Yet 380 nulls at 0.0019 each give at least one with chance $1 - 0.9981^{380} \approx 0.51$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A share of finds and the chance of at least one false find are different things.

byKey.fwer: That is the share of finds that are false. With 380 independent nulls at 0.0019 each, the chance of at least one false find is $1 - 0.9981^{380} \approx 0.51$.
byKey.per-find: 0.0019 is the chance that a null passes, not the share of finds that are false.
byKey.none: 0.722 false finds are still expected, and one or more happens in about half of all fields.

explain.text: A false share is an average over finds. It does not say that no false find occurs: with so many nulls, one or more is more likely than not.
